explanation:
The inspection confirms the reference rule reproduces all four train outputs exactly, and gives a sensible result on the test input, so I'll keep its logic and explain it.

## What the grids are made of

Every input has two layers:

- A **blue (1) wall** running from the left edge to the right edge. It is not straight: it has rectangular notches cut out of it from below (the places where the wall rises up and comes back down). In train 1 the notches are a 2×2 pocket at rows 2–3, cols 3–4 and a 1-wide, 2-tall slot at (2,9),(3,9). In train 4 there is a single 2×2 pocket at rows 5–6, cols 6–7. These notches are the "recesses".
- Several **gray (5) pieces** sitting below the wall: small polyominoes of 3–8 cells.

The output keeps the wall and leaves every piece where it is; the only change is that some pieces turn **red (2)** while others stay gray. So this is an object-classification puzzle: which property of a piece decides red vs gray?

## Finding the property

Comparing the pieces with the recesses makes the pattern clear:

- Train 4: the 2×2 gray square becomes red (the recess is a 2×2 pocket, which the square plugs exactly); the vertical 1×3 bar stays gray (a 1-wide bar can't fill a 2-wide pocket).
- Train 2: the recess is again 2×2. The 2×2 square is red; the P-shaped 5-cell piece (a 2×2 block with one extra cell) is red; the S/Z tetromino stays gray — no rotation of an S-tetromino covers a 2×2 square.
- Train 1: recesses are a 2×2 pocket and a 1×2 vertical slot. The 2×2 square → red; the 1-wide vertical 3-bar → red (it plugs the slot, poking one cell above); the big 8-cell piece (3×3 block minus corners, i.e. with a protruding cell) → red (rotated, it covers the 2×2 pocket with its extra bulk sticking through); the S-tetromino → gray.
- Train 3: recesses are an L-shaped 3-cell notch and a T-shaped 4-cell notch. The L-tromino becomes red (it fits the L notch after rotation) and the plus-shaped piece becomes red (its top covers the T-notch, matching recess shapes). The 1×3 bar and the J-shaped 4-cell piece stay gray.

So the rule: **a gray piece is painted red if, after some rotation, it can be placed so that it covers every cell of one recess without overlapping any blue cell.** The extra cells of the piece may extend upward through the opening (that's the only place they can go, since the recess is enclosed on the sides and above by blue... well, above the wall is open space). Pieces that can't plug any recess stay gray. Nothing moves — the recolouring is just a marking of "this piece would fit."

I verified this with code: computing the recesses as the below-wall background cells lying at or above the wall's lowest row, then testing each piece with all 4 rotations against every recess, reproduces all four train outputs cell for cell.

## Applying to the test input

The test wall (rows 2–4) has an L-shaped recess {(3,2),(4,2),(4,3)} and a 1×2 vertical slot {(3,8),(4,8)}. The gray pieces:

- 5-cell piece at cols 4–5 (a vertical bar with a bump): with a rotation it covers the L-recess → red.
- S-shaped piece at cols 1–2: it covers the L-recess (the L is a subset of an S tetromino) → red.
- 1×3 vertical bar at col 10: plugs the vertical slot → red.
- 2×2 square at cols 7–8: a 2×2 block can't sit in a 1-wide slot and can't cover the L without overlapping blue → stays gray.
